section.title: David Singleton: From Symbian to Stripe CTO, Engineering Leadership, and Hiring Without LeetCode
section.deck: David Singleton, a former Google VP of engineering and Stripe CTO, describes how continuous learning, deliberate organizational design and engineering-system investments shaped their career, and why Stripe hired by pair programming instead of whiteboard puzzles.

blocks.text: David Singleton, who describes a path from Symbian engineer to Google VP of engineering to Stripe CTO and now founder of a consumer AI-agent platform called Dev Agents, argues for a few connected ideas. Keep learning, and choose roles by what you want from the work rather than by the next rung of a ladder. Leaders at any level should still experience the team's work at close range. A team that is perfectly happy is rarely performing at its best. Organizations improve when their rituals, operating principles and release systems are designed on purpose. Reliability and speed can rise together through automated testing and gradual deployment. Stripe hired engineers by pairing with them on realistic work instead of using whiteboard puzzles. And the most useful career advice Singleton offers is to speak up when you know something. Everything below is Singleton's own account and opinion, as told to the host in a career-story interview. The framing in this paragraph is editorial.
blocks.heading: Learn on purpose, test what you want from the work, and run an organization as a designed system

blocks.question: How did Singleton get into programming?
answer: Singleton got into computers as a child in the late 1980s or early 1990s, when a computer arrived in the household for the parents' business. Singleton taught themselves to code. Many children of that era learned to write games, but Singleton wrote bespoke business software for the family firm, starting with an invoicing system.

The system mattered because, before it, the parents tabulated invoices for their tax returns by hand. Singleton and a sibling had noticed the parents turning grumpy once a quarter because they were up all night on the accounts. After the software, one button press produced the invoices from the printer. Singleton says this showed that software can have a large effect on people, and that effect, more than the technology itself, is what led to studying computer science and entering the industry.
blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What was it like to start a career at Symbian?
answer: Singleton had planned to return to Northern Ireland and join a software company in Belfast, but that firm went under in the internet bust. Stuck in Cambridge, England, and needing a job at short notice, Singleton met some Symbian employees, liked them, and applied. Symbian built smartphone operating system software around 2001, before smartphones were a mainstream product. Singleton says they went for the people but quickly found that the team believed smartphones were inevitable and that the work would change how people used computers. The team was inventing things now taken for granted, such as sketching how turn-by-turn map directions would plug into the operating system once GPS chips reached handsets.

Singleton started as a software engineer building core parts of the Bluetooth stack and some PC-connection software. In the last couple of years, Singleton became a technical consultant. This was still an individual-contributor role, but it meant working with teams at handset makers who were turning the Symbian OS into products. Singleton was the technical lead on the Symbian side of essentially the same project repeated at companies such as Panasonic in the US, Samsung in Korea and China, and Nokia in Finland. Help varied by team: setting up source control for the first time at one, debugging a graphics problem at another.

Singleton says seeing how team culture shaped what got built, this early, left a lasting interest in how teams are organized. From memory, and noting that those companies surely work differently now, Samsung ran very small teams and gave several teams the same mission, with the first to finish getting to ship. Nokia planned everything in much more intricate detail, which made things predictable but significantly slower.

followups.question: Was the technical consultant role similar to today's forward deployed engineer?
answer: Singleton had not thought of it that way but calls it a good observation. People in the role helped customers integrate the product into their own handsets and also brought customer insights and questions back to inform Symbian's roadmap. Nobody used the term then. Singleton enjoyed the role, travelled the world, and found it rewarding, though says they would not want to do it now.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: How did Singleton end up at Google, and why stay so long?
answer: Singleton was in London working for Symbian shortly after Google's IPO. According to Singleton, Symbian had already recognised that smartphones would matter for how people reached online services, and London was then a recognised centre of mobile expertise, so Google opened a mobile-focused engineering office there. Singleton attended a recruiting event and went through what they call a tough interview process, including a first-ever trip to California. The quality of the people and the energy of the company convinced Singleton this was the next place to be.

Singleton never imagined staying nearly 12 years. The plan was to learn how to build distributed systems at scale and see the best engineering in the industry, then take that elsewhere. Every 18 months or two years, Singleton would look up and realise they had learned a tremendous amount, so stayed. The host observed that people with long, successful tenures at one company often are not complacent. They are nearly trying to leave, but the place treats them well enough that they stay. Singleton says they had about six different jobs at Google, with very gradual transitions between them.

followups.question: What did early Google offer that made it such a good place to learn?
answer: Singleton describes remarkable talent density, a drive to have impact, and a lot of autonomy. The 20 percent culture was real. Singleton did the work the manager and team expected and was welcome to pick up many other things, and treated that as the chance to learn as much as possible.

One example came while Singleton worked on a Google Maps feature for mobile, before Android. Every mobile visit to google.com was redirected to google.com/m, and with the mobile network round-trip times of the day that could cost about two and a half seconds. Co-workers said fixing it was too hard because it lived in front-end infrastructure nobody on the team knew. Singleton, determined that it was just software, chased it partly to learn how that infrastructure worked, and eventually merged a change into the main Google web server that removed the redirect. By Singleton's own rough calculation this saved something like 70 years of user time per year, and Singleton believes it had a noticeable effect on usage. The lesson Singleton draws is the fun of following your nose to learn and taking agency to do things that matter.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: Was it perceived impact or technical curiosity that drove that agency?
answer: Early on, Singleton says, it was technical curiosity, with little sense of how many people the work reached. A product manager colleague, who is Icelandic, began restating the product's active users in terms of national populations. One week the product matched the population of Iceland, then Ireland, then Scotland, and eventually Germany. Singleton says Google taught them to think about how many people they could affect, and that has been the real driver of everything since.

The host compared this to a YouTube goal of a billion minutes watched, which gave everyone a big unifying number to chase. Singleton agrees that a clearly defined, achievable but audacious goal helps a team rally and do remarkable things, something Singleton experienced as an engineer and later used as a manager.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What led Singleton from individual contributor to manager so quickly?
answer: Singleton was an engineer having a great time and was surrounded by product managers who helped the team see its impact. Singleton walked into the manager's office and said they wanted to be a product manager. The manager suggested engineering management instead, arguing it would give similar fulfilment from impact while keeping technical work. Google then had a role called TLM, or 'Uber tech lead', and Singleton found the choice easy. Singleton acknowledges that the team needed managers, so they were also solving the manager's problem, but says they get real energy from helping people do more together.

Singleton stayed deep in the details, writing code and designs, and over time managed several teams at once, with management taking most of the normal work day. Google encouraged its 20 percent time, and for a couple of years Singleton managed teams during the day and then worked on personal engineering projects once people went home, at a time when Singleton's spouse had a very busy job. One of those projects was the first version of Google Translate on the iPhone. Singleton's advice for anyone who loves code but wants managerial impact is that if you can find a place to do both, it can be very fulfilling, and if something gives you energy, go at it.

followups.question: Most people who tried the TLM role say it means doing two jobs and excelling at neither. Why are you supportive?
answer: Singleton understands that view. The projects Singleton managed were different from the ones Singleton worked on as an individual contributor. Singleton thinks it is harder when you are the individual contributor on a project you also manage, which Singleton is doing now at the startup and enjoying. It is easy to get sucked into your own work and lose track of what each person on the team needs in order to be unblocked, so you need a constant prompt to switch modes.

Years later at Stripe, a management coach, Jeff Lawrence, gave Singleton an analogy: a leader must repeatedly step from the dance floor onto the balcony and look down at how everything is working. Singleton says that applies to TLMs too. It is a hard role to make work, but possible if you deliberately create moments in the week and day for that step.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: As a VP at Google, was Singleton still doing feature work?
answer: Not as a critical contributor, Singleton says. But Singleton believes deeply, and took the idea to Stripe, that however senior you are, effective leaders find a way to experience the team's work at what Singleton calls the one-foot level. As VP of engineering running Android Wear, which Singleton describes as the foundation of the wearables platform in Google smartwatches and which Singleton ran almost like a general manager across product, engineering, partnerships, user experience and marketing, Singleton found it valuable to experience the toolchain the engineers used. Roughly every two or three months Singleton did a small project in the codebase, which made it easier to ask smart questions and see what was needed to unblock people.

followups.question: Why not hand the hands-on project to someone else, given the debate about managers coding?
answer: Singleton separates two moments. The iPhone Translate project came in the first year as a TLM, when doing a real project end to end was appropriate for keeping skills sharp. As a leader of managers, coding the whole time would be damaging, because the job is giving teams context, unblocking work, building partnerships and working across a large company. Singleton says that is about 95 percent of where time must go. Still, Singleton has a belief grounded in experience that carving out deliberate time to work in the same mode as the teams gives tremendous context. Singleton compares it to a manufacturing practice of managers and senior leaders working a day on the factory floor.

At Stripe, Singleton did this at least once a quarter, except perhaps the busy final quarter, joining a team for a few days to finish a small real project. Singleton called it 'engineeration', a blend of engineer and vacation. Singleton told colleagues to treat the days as a vacation, reachable for a crisis but otherwise not to be disturbed. Each time Singleton wrote a detailed friction log of everything frustrating, which fed Singleton's thinking as CTO about where to invest in developer productivity and helped in asking good questions in operational reviews. Singleton encouraged other managers to do it. Not everyone did, but those who did found it valuable. Singleton suggests it for anyone in a large organization who feels out of touch.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: So the iOS project was hands-on contribution, while engineeration is more an educational exercise for yourself?
answer: Singleton agrees and adds that it is also a chance to show others what you saw. The reports from engineeration gave context to other managers, helping them correct mental models, especially as the infrastructure changed over time. Singleton calls that educational use the heart of its value.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: Were you ever afraid of losing your technical edge?
answer: Not really, Singleton says. Singleton loves programming and gets into a flow state doing it. Between pieces of code at work and personal time, the skills stayed alive. Right now Singleton programs plenty at work and has little spare time. When there is spare time and Singleton has not coded in a while, they jump in, for example by doing Advent of Code each December for the last several years.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What is the best way to decide between becoming a manager and staying an individual contributor?
answer: Singleton agrees with the advice that managing and individual contribution are different jobs and should not be done together, and has given that advice to many people. If you are considering management, Singleton suggests finding an environment where you can do it full time, set your own individual work aside, and pay close attention to what makes the team productive and happy. People who do it that way tend to thrive, while doing both is harder unless carefully structured. A company willing to let you try management on a trial basis is fortunate, and Singleton recommends taking that option if it exists.

When people tell Singleton they want to go into management, Singleton often first tries to talk them out of it. Singleton says that ten years ago, though less so now, there was an odd incentive structure in which managing ever-larger teams was seen as the prize. Companies such as Google and Meta have since cultivated career ladders that let individual contributors progress very far. Being a manager who feels fulfilled requires getting a lot of energy from getting more out of other people, and that is not for everybody. Singleton advises reflecting on whether that excites you and, if so, trying it.

followups.question: For someone set on going up the ladder, which path would you recommend?
answer: Singleton chose to answer differently. Early and mid-career at Google, there was a clear level structure, and Singleton admits playing it for a while, which luckily matched what gave them energy. After talking with many people and reflecting on later experience, Singleton concluded that the way to get the most fulfilment is to work out what you want from the work. It might be the flow state of coding, impact on very many people, or a strong bond with a team. Singleton advises stepping aside from the obvious games companies set up and asking what you are trying to get, which might be the next rung or something quite different. Singleton says they worked this out around the time of thinking about leaving Google and feels significantly more fulfilled since.
The host noted that some people will chase the carrot regardless, which is fine as long as they chase the right one.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: When you moved from frontline manager to manager of managers, what was your biggest skill gap?
answer: Singleton thinks they learned the wrong lessons as a very early manager. With a single team, you can do everything to make that team happy, which is not the same as getting the best impact from it, and the team may not look back on that time as the best of their careers. Singleton won Google's 'great manager award' while managing one team, an award voted on by the teams themselves, and says they did not deserve it.

As a manager of managers, Singleton learned that teams that are perfectly happy are rarely performing at their potential. For the biggest impact, low performers have to be managed directly, and you cannot make a whole team happy unless people feel surrounded by colleagues who pull their weight. Singleton saw some managers who understood the goal, cleared distractions, and pushed their team a little, and others doing what Singleton used to do. Singleton's answer was to help the latter get more from their teams, and to step onto the balcony more often to see how the whole group configured itself.

The tools change too. A line manager needs good one-to-ones, one-to-one documents and goals, and some craft coaching. A manager of managers can think about the systems of the organization, such as product reviews and the hiring process, and Singleton says they were lucky to be able to change these at each stage. As a software and distributed-systems enthusiast, Singleton found it exciting to treat the organization as something like an operating system, asking how everything done daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly and yearly fits together. Singleton calls this a whole new toolkit that a line manager does not think about.

followups.question: Is a team that is too happy a red flag for you?
answer: Singleton does not want anyone unhappy and aspires to build organizations where Singleton would happily do any job in them. But over time Singleton has compared teams reporting the greatest happiness with teams that said they were pretty happy but offered lots of feedback on what could go better. A year later, Singleton says, the second group, who wanted to change things and were put in a position to think about their impact, tended in retrospect to have had the best time.

At Stripe, Singleton learned the term type two fun, the fun you remember as some of the best times of your life but that is hard in the moment. Singleton wants to create a lot of it for the teams they work with, while keeping it sustainable. The host added that teams that never break anything are probably moving too slowly, and Singleton called that a great analogy.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What changed between being a very senior manager and being a VP?
answer: Singleton says this varies by person, but for them the defining change was taking responsibility for functions beyond engineering. The title was VP of engineering, but by then Google paid little attention to job family and cared about assembling the full set of skills needed to get something done. This changed Singleton's perspective. Earlier in a company Singleton regards as engineering-first in those days, Singleton had thought the other functions existed to feed engineers. Singleton now says that is not true. Without other functions to help ensure you solve the right problem, get the right user input and make the right business deals, you will have less fun and less impact.

It was also a personal adjustment. When you manage a function you have worked in, you have a visceral sense of how to do the work. Singleton has designers reporting to them and calls themself a pretty lousy designer who would do badly in Figma. Singleton still had to learn to lead them well, and found they care a lot about design and can have high-bandwidth conversations about it. The hard part was gaining confidence that being unable to jump into any seat in the organization and perform the job did not stop them from leading. Singleton calls this the biggest transition of that jump.

followups.question: Did you ever apply the engineeration idea to other roles?
answer: At Stripe, one team in the technology organization built tools for sales, so Singleton did the equivalent, which they called a sales-occasion, shadowing a couple of salespeople. Singleton mostly did it to gain context for prioritising engineering work, and found it very useful. Singleton would not do it identically for every role. For design, Singleton says it would be more a matter of shadowing someone than jumping in to do all the work.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: How should an engineering leader get better at communication?
answer: Singleton splits communication into speaking and writing. For speaking to large audiences, the number one method is practice. Early on, Singleton was quite nervous presenting to a large internal audience, and a supportive manager responded by giving more chances to practice. That led to speaking to a whole auditorium of Google customers while Singleton was working on ads. Singleton recalls one in London, near King's Cross, with maybe a thousand people, a live demo and an inspirational talk about local ads. It was scary, but Singleton did it, and says repetition is what makes it go well.

On writing, Singleton says they are still learning and uses Claude a lot. Condensing the most important points into a short clear document is valuable, Singleton argues. Speaking to a large audience may reach perhaps 30 percent who are really listening, and people forget. A good document gets passed around, read, and revisited, so it is a highly leveraged way to communicate at scale. But Singleton thinks both are needed: people listen to those they have a personal relationship with, which comes from live conversation, and once that exists, written material scales easily.

followups.question: How did you get the stage presence the host saw in your 2019 Stripe Sessions keynote?
answer: Singleton credits practice and the manager who pushed for it, saying that on that stage in 2012, people would have thought Singleton was out of their depth. Singleton adds that a senior leader is effectively always on stage in the office. People take confidence in the company's plans from the CTO's body language, so a hallway chat or a random meeting is another chance to remind people what the company is doing and why.

Singleton also advises having dynamic range. If everything is always awesome, no one believes you when it truly is awesome. If everything is always bleak, you cannot get people excited about crossing the hill. Before speaking in any meeting, big or small, Singleton took a moment to think about what they were actually trying to communicate.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: Most engineers asked to give an all-hands talk lose the room. How can a manager tell stories that hold attention?
answer: First, prepare. Singleton says they have often made the mistake of agreeing to show up and give their top of mind, when the real answer was that they were hungry. If an audience spends 15 or 20 minutes listening, Singleton argues, the speaker can spend 30 minutes preparing and deciding what context is most useful for them.

Second, Singleton describes a Google leader, Alan Eustace, who answered questions by first stepping back to explain the context behind the question and why it mattered, so people unfamiliar with the problem could follow and learn something broader. Singleton aspires to that. It also helps with a story arc: say why it matters, then the point, then perhaps a detail, then remind people what you said. Singleton notes that this is a trick for writing as well.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: How important is having people review your writing?
answer: Singleton learned this at Stripe. Singleton used to write blog posts, such as one about a neural-network-controlled car that got a lot of coverage, and publish them directly. At Stripe, Singleton saw good authors crediting their reviewers, started sending drafts of important pieces to others, and says the quality of the writing improved immensely. An author carries a mental model of what the reader knows, and reviewers, including friends and former co-workers, often ask questions the author would not have thought of. Singleton clarifies that this is not for every email, only for an important message you really want to land.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What are high-leverage ways for a senior leader to scale beyond coaching direct reports?
answer: Singleton points to the organization's rituals and processes. As an early-career engineer, Singleton thought 'process' was a dirty word, partly because of Symbian's process library, a quality-certification practice in which people were meant to look up and follow documented processes. In practice nobody did, and people filled out the paperwork afterwards if someone asked. When Singleton became an organizational leader and was told to think about processes, the first reaction was dismay. Reasoning from first principles, Singleton realised the point was the rituals and ways of working through which things get done, and that getting them right is very impactful.

As an example, Singleton set up, with help from colleagues, a set of meetings at Stripe called ops review. A weekly one run by Singleton looked at the most important matters, and a nested set ran across all engineering teams in the company. Singleton says this helped the whole company pay attention to and improve things such as reliability and efficiency, which would have been hard to move just by talking to direct reports and letting the message trickle down.

followups.question: How do you decide whether a process is a net positive or net negative?
answer: Singleton says the person responsible for running a process must make sure it exists only while it is clearly a net positive for everyone operating it. Singleton sees an organizational-design trap in some companies, and does not mean Stripe, where the person who oversees a process is not the person who cared about it or introduced it to solve a problem. Because it is their assigned job, it is hard for them to ask whether it is still fit for purpose. Singleton says leaders of large organizations should avoid that, since there is always plenty of work and nobody should feel boxed into continuing something for no reason.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: If you hand a process top down to a tech lead, how do you keep them passionate about it?
answer: Singleton believes it is possible to build teams of program managers who are passionate about the why. Singleton helped set up Stripe's program management group and says the vast majority were focused on doing the right thing and on impact for Stripe's users. Much of that comes from company culture, whose first operating principle is users first, so people always ask why the work matters.

The host added that how you delegate matters. Singleton agreed: telling someone to 'do this' leaves them nothing but to do it, while describing the problem, suggesting a direction and asking them to take agency in solving the real problem produces completely different outcomes.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: How do you get a remote engineering site to carry the right culture, drawing on London?
answer: The host noted that the Facebook London site lead had credited Singleton with the best advice on starting that site. Singleton explains that they led Google's London engineering site while the other person led Facebook's, so they were in a fierce battle for talent, often discovering that both had offers out to the same candidate. The other site lead eventually reached out, and Singleton admires that. Singleton values a Silicon Valley attitude in which fierce competitors still help each other with the craft, and believes the two helped raise the engineering bar in London.

For a site far from headquarters, such as London to Mountain View with perhaps one hour of daily overlap, Singleton pushed for teams to be able to unblock themselves and run autonomously, so they use the overlap for as few things as possible. Every London team needed a clear and complete mission, a lot of autonomy, and all the equipment to execute on its own. The worst arrangement, Singleton says, would be half a team in each place, because the hundred daily conversations needed to unblock work would not fit the time window. A site in the same time zone, like Stripe's Seattle office relative to San Francisco, can be set up quite differently.

Singleton also describes an earlier London site lead who rarely sat in London and explained that the best thing for the site was to be in Mountain View, building personal relationships and bringing context back. Singleton later did the same, travelling to California a lot so others did not have to, and making sure the team's capabilities were visible, such as London's experts who had worked on WebKit.

Finally, Singleton says every effective remote site had a bit of its own culture. A sense of identity makes people willing to spend energy fixing friction, because they are part of a clan. But the culture must not be radically different from the whole company's, or people start to see the other side of the ocean as fools. The trick is enough identity for people to help each other, rooted in the company culture. In reply to the host's prompt, Singleton confirms this meant t-shirts and laptop logos and gatherings to discuss what work the site was good at, which Singleton then carried to California.

followups.question: After COVID, is in-person, remote or hybrid best for a team?
answer: Singleton notes that Stripe had a remote hub well before COVID because it recognised strong technical talent exists everywhere. That led to deliberate thought about making remote teams effective. One key is a culture of document-based communication and decision-making: conversations between individuals on a video call or in person were written up for the rest of the team, and critical decisions came with a document. Singleton says that can be slower for a given decision, though not always, because writing forces useful deliberation, and it lets everyone understand the context, contribute and buy in.

Singleton also says nothing replaces time in person to build rapport, but not every day. Meeting on a cadence, perhaps every six months, can help remote teams work very well. Remote can be almost as effective for some teams, but Singleton personally believes the best is everyone together in one place. The Dev Agents team is small and based together in San Francisco, which Singleton thinks suits this stage. As the company grows, Singleton expects to revisit that, because some excellent people cannot move, and says it is hard to build a huge company today without leaning into distributed offices and remote work.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What kept Singleton in the VP role for two years and five months, and why leave Google?
answer: Singleton's short answer is unfinished business. Google made Singleton a VP not long after the first version of Android Wear shipped, and Singleton had exciting plans in motion with handset and watch manufacturers and wanted to see them through. Singleton was also still learning, including by managing some of the new functions mentioned earlier, and says staying anywhere that long is justified only while you keep learning.

About two years later, Singleton realised they were very happy and deeply grateful to Google, but that the last year had been the same as the year before with different project code names. They had not learned much, and learning is what they were there for. That was the wake-up call. Around then Singleton also had conversations with a good friend, Philip, about starting a company together and realised it would be an amazing learning experience, which pushed Singleton to think it was time for the next move.

followups.question: Philip was a rival site lead you competed with for talent. Why consider starting a company together?
answer: Singleton says they had found a lot of mutual respect, and that is among the best relationships to form in business. Singleton feels privileged to have bonded with someone who was sometimes on the other side of the table.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What was the company idea, and how did that lead to Stripe?
answer: Singleton and Philip had an idea Singleton still thinks is good. Singleton had noticed the rise of the gig economy and had a side project making journals to sell, for which they needed legal help and a graphic designer, both hard to find. Platforms like Fiverr helped with some design work. The idea was to let professionals in job families such as legal and graphic design benefit from gig-style flexibility while also getting the stability and benefits of working for a firm. Fractional professionals would be recruited onto a platform and employed by the firm, which would invest in their professional development and give them varied work and career growth.

They did not start it then, because of complicated personal circumstances and a sense that it was not the right moment, and because Singleton began talking to people at Stripe. Singleton says they were struck by Stripe's mission to increase the GDP of the internet, which is about helping entrepreneurs start and scale companies, create jobs and move money in new ways. That resonated with Singleton's own start in software, building an invoicing system for a small business. To Singleton's surprise, much of what Stripe needed to scale was what they had done before, such as running Google's London engineering office, when Stripe was looking to open engineering offices around the world, and building new products. Singleton says they fell in love with the mission and joined.

followups.question: When did the advice conversation turn into recruiting?
answer: Singleton did first reach out for advice. They quote someone's saying that when you want money you should ask for advice, and when you want advice you should ask for money. Singleton first found that cynical but has seen it prove right. Singleton wanted to learn about Stripe Connect, which powers two-sided marketplaces and was an obvious tool for the planned company, and thought Stripe people might even invest. The first conversation was valuable advice. Then Patrick, whom Singleton identifies as Stripe's co-founder and CEO, said they would be in town soon and suggested meeting. Singleton still thought it was advice, but presumes Patrick approached it as a hiring conversation from the start. Singleton quickly found they wanted Stripe to be the next chapter.

Having since hired senior executives, Singleton says the process is very custom, though it also needs a systematic approach. The people who will be a good fit are usually committed to something already, so you identify them, get on their radar, start with an advice conversation, help them see the opportunity, and vet along the way to ensure they will supercharge the team. Singleton calls the transition from getting-to-know-you to seeing-if-it-fits a real art, and a fun one.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: How did a head-of-engineering role become CTO?
answer: Singleton says they cared little about the title when joining. What mattered was joining the core leadership team and having enough agency to help the company get the things done that it needed. The role was never very formal, and later the company decided to give it the CTO title, mostly to signal that Singleton was worth listening to. This was around when Singleton started running companywide processes, and it helped in engaging customers and partners outside the company, where titles start to matter. Singleton prefers a culture where people are not listened to because of a title, which Singleton says is Stripe's culture, but accepts that titles matter when dealing with the outside world.

The host said organizations inside large companies are almost strangers, so a director reaching out helps get alignment. Singleton recalled that when made a director at Google, new directors were sent on a training course where they were told, and Singleton does not know whether this was true, that directors really run the company, because that is where detailed plans pass between teams. Singleton takes from this that org design should include a network of people ensuring high-fidelity context transfer, which at Google then was directors.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: Which big tech company has the best-designed engineering culture?
answer: Singleton says they are at a disadvantage, having worked only at Google among the big companies and knowing the others by reputation. Google's culture, in Singleton's account, was phenomenal: everyone was there to do big things, was encouraged to have impact, and was given a lot of agency. But Singleton does not think it was very deliberately designed. It was not chaos, and there was an org structure, but it grew mostly organically.

In contrast, as Stripe designed its org structure and ways of working while scaling, Singleton looked to companies that had been deliberate, especially Amazon. Singleton talked to many senior leaders there. The ops review that Stripe ran, and still runs, was modelled on Amazon's. Singleton recalls Charlie Bell spending a lunch walking through how it worked, and Stripe took the parts that fit its size and culture. Singleton calls Amazon the company with the systematic organizational and operational design that has most inspired them, though they never worked there.

Singleton says they would love to work at each such company for one project to experience it. Apple, for example, builds products Singleton loves, is not very transparent inside, and is deliberate about its org structure, with an Apple University where joiners learn to work the Apple way. This reminds Singleton of dealing with the mobile handset makers at the start of their career and seeing many ways to reach the same ends. Singleton would like to choose from the smorgasbord, but has only worked at one big company and gone deep with leaders at one other.
blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: Stripe's operating principles seem to echo Amazon's. How are operating principles different from values?
answer: The host saw a similarity between Stripe's first principle, users first, and Amazon's customer obsession. Singleton agrees: users first means everything is aimed at understanding why the work matters to the user, a maxim Singleton lives by. Singleton explains that operating principles differ from values. After the early Stripe team found product-market fit in its core business, payment infrastructure for early-stage companies, they stepped aside and asked what about how they worked made them most effective. The resulting principles are concrete, distilled from the behaviour of the most effective Stripes, and revisited from time to time, so they can change.

The principle that most motivated Singleton is being meticulous in your craft: taking pride in how well things are done for their own sake, which means well-designed systems, reliable services, polished edges, and having external people review a blog post before publishing. Singleton accepts that this looks hard to justify with numbers, but says it has a dramatic and hard-to-quantify effect on how products are perceived. Singleton often met CTOs of very large Stripe customers who said they did the integration when small and were inspired by Stripe's error messages.

As an example, Singleton describes how the Stripe API handles a test mode and a production mode. When an integration switches modes, a resource request often fails because the object lives in the other mode. Rather than the bare 404 most engineers would build first, Stripe's API runs extra code and says the resource was not found but an object with that ID exists in the other mode. Singleton says people remember this kind of attention. The broader point is that being deliberate about the operating principles behind your success is very useful.
blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: At what company stage should you start thinking about culture, and how does a leader enforce it?
answer: Singleton is building a very early-stage company and thinks culture matters from day one. On the day they incorporated, Singleton and the co-founders went for a drink and wrote down their values, which they have used in hiring and in how they run things. Because an early-stage company often gets 'smacked in the face' by surprises, values help show where to compromise and where not to. Singleton says it would be too early to schedule a weekly culture activity, and at this stage culture should be organic. But in later-stage companies you need to be intentional, because companies are large groups of people, and without something that brings them together with shared purpose and alignment, entropy takes over. If you do not invest in culture, Singleton says, you almost by definition will not have one. Singleton notes that intentional organizations such as Stripe and Amazon tend to be very effective, and that some companies they worked at early on, which were not intentional, have not lasted.

followups.question: Concretely, how does an engineering leader enforce culture?
answer: Singleton names two ways. The first is to be an authentic exemplar, which means working at a place whose culture you identify with and living it. Singleton was at Stripe because they cared about its mission, its users and being meticulous in the craft, and says it would have been hard not to show up and use that culture. In an environment with values at odds with Singleton's own, Singleton would not have lasted so long.

The second is to accept that the culture is whatever behaviour you tolerate. Singleton first heard a teammate say that culture is the behaviours you accept, found it pessimistic, and then found it true. If people see you witness something out of line and say nothing, that becomes the culture, so Singleton believes in being, as pleasantly and upbeat as possible, a bit of a police officer for culture. Singleton gives an example of a senior leader who walked past a spilled drink on the stairs, then stopped, went to the kitchen and cleaned it up despite more important work. Only a few people saw it, but the story spread, signalling that it was worth their time to clean up after others.

At Stripe, Singleton also made it easy to report bugs through a mailing list that many people subscribed to, then sent examples that fell below the bar to it, supportively and sometimes with a suggested copy change. Later the company set up 'walk the store', using the product live in companywide meetings, sometimes run by Singleton and sometimes by others, not to call people out but to show what the company aspired to. The host called that potentially nerve-wracking.

Singleton also describes friction logging, which they learned at Stripe and use at Dev Agents. Leaders, or anyone, can regularly put on the user's hat, perhaps weekly, monthly or every six weeks, use the product, and write down everything frustrating or odd, then use that to set the team's priorities. Even teams whose users are internal can do this. At Dev Agents the team uses everything every week and writes meticulous friction logs to decide what to work on next, which also shows what is good enough and where the bar sits.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What intentional engineering-culture changes enabled Stripe's many nines of reliability?
answer: Singleton says Stripe reached more than five nines of reliability during their tenure and that they have heard it reached six nines last quarter. These are Singleton's figures and are not verified here. For a payments business, every second of downtime costs businesses real money, so reliability matters greatly. Singleton says it started with being intentional. The pandemic in 2020 brought a rush of offline businesses online, and Stripe's systems were scaling much faster than expected, so the company knew it had to raise the bar. The engineering organization had not been wired for that. Earlier it had rightly focused on product-market fit, with emergencies fixed as they came, but at scale reliability mattered. Singleton calls the change mostly cultural.

Singleton's approach was to give every team the tools to reason scientifically about trade-offs between feature work and reliability work. That meant ops review plus a nested set of systems, meetings and data tools, and repeated chances to look at the data and decide what to do. In short, build conviction that it matters, set up a repeatable system so everyone has the right input, and look at it often enough to act. Because everything was measured systematically and surfaced widely, Singleton says, progress also came on efficiency and performance.

followups.question: Reliability costs redundancy and review overhead. Did you ever ask whether Stripe was too reliable for the cost?
answer: Singleton says that at Stripe the change made the system significantly more efficient as well. Speaking industry-wide, Singleton sees at least two reasons systems are unreliable. One is trying to serve more demand than capacity, where you might over-provision, and where you may also not have invested enough in graceful degradation and partial availability. The other is a lack of guard rails to stop legitimate engineering changes from breaking things, and the fix there is entirely different.

Stripe invested heavily in automated testing and gradual deployment. There were periods of extra reviews, but the investment let the whole organization go faster. Singleton's lesson is to build great automated testing and gradual deployment so failures are caught before they are critical, for code, data and feature flags alike, and to ask the five whys about whatever causes problems. In this case, Singleton says, there were few trade-offs in productivity and none in efficiency.

The result was that a change merged to main went to production, usually the same day, through an automated gradual release process. At Google, by contrast, a release branch was cut roughly every two weeks, tested partly by hand and patched with cherry-picks, and then sat in production for two weeks, so a change could take about a month to be fully live. Singleton says it is hard to iterate that way and much more fun to show a same-day change to co-workers. The host summarised that shifting left removes the trade-off between de-risking and speed, and Singleton agreed and recommended the book Accelerate by Nicole Forsgren.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What did Stripe do to hire such strong engineers without relying on LeetCode-style interviews?
answer: Singleton starts with attraction. Many strong engineers wanted to work at Stripe and reached out, usually because they had a good experience with the product. At its core Stripe is a developer platform with a deserved reputation for some of the best documentation in the industry. Stripe treated documentation as part of building the product, written by the product teams rather than a separate team, with nicely designed APIs and pride in presentation. So, Singleton says, ship a great product and people will want to work on it.

On evaluation, Singleton says the industry was still doing a lot of whiteboard interviews when they joined, and all of Singleton's own interviews before Stripe were of that kind. Stripe believed, and Singleton still believes, that writing code on a whiteboard is not a great way to simulate seeing an engineer do real work. So Stripe designed a process in which candidates used a laptop with their usual tools and pair programmed with an interviewer, to give the most realistic experience of work possible. The exercises were deliberately designed to select for people who wanted to be meticulous in their craft and had the core engineering, design and inquisitive skills to find what needed doing. Singleton credits this with maintaining the talent bar for years.

followups.question: LeetCode-style questions are said to be used at the largest companies because questions leak at scale. How did Stripe manage?
answer: Singleton admits it was hard work. Interview questions do leak online, and once that happens you need a new one to assess people fairly rather than reward those who searched beforehand. A decent number of engineers at Stripe were passionate about this and got others passionate too, so building the questions was a volunteer effort. Singleton says leaders must make sure contributors are recognised: Singleton thanked them at engineering all-hands, and the work contributed to their advancement, alongside doing their core job well.

Singleton adds that if Meta or Google say they lack the resources to build good engineering interviews, Singleton does not believe it. In Singleton's view, they could do it if they wanted to, and it is a revealed preference about how much they care. Singleton stresses that both are amazing companies and this is not criticism, only that real care makes the hard work possible.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: So to attract excellent people, build something excellent?
answer: Singleton calls it neither necessary nor sufficient. You can probably attract great people to something that is not great by paying above market, but people are really excited to work on something demonstrably awesome, and Singleton would rather take that route. It is not sufficient, because candidates also need to see that they can learn, advance their career goals and be surrounded by people they want to spend their precious hours with. Singleton says it certainly goes a long way.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What did Singleton learn most from the Stripe leadership team?
answer: Singleton says the biggest lesson from friends and peers on the leadership team was the value of thinking from first principles, something Singleton was not good at when joining. At Google, which invented many of the ways of working in the industry, Singleton's habit was to ask how it had been done last time and reuse it. At Stripe the constant refrain, when facing a problem, was to ask what is actually going on and to understand the dynamics. A related technique was to ask people at several external companies how they had handled similar problems and triangulate. Singleton says that can sound slow, but applied to the most consequential problems it brings the benefit of multiple perspectives, and Singleton still does it.

followups.question: Surely at your stage you can sometimes shortcut and use experience instead of first principles?
answer: Singleton thinks it is remarkable how often it pays to step back, reason from first principles and check yourself on whether you have really seen this before. Singleton's rough sense, an estimate rather than data, is that 80 percent of the time it is something you have seen and you can just go do it, while 20 percent of the time it is subtly different and worth getting other opinions. Singleton agrees it is not a tool for everything every day, or everything would grind to a halt.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: Why did Singleton leave Stripe to build Dev Agents, and what is it building?
answer: Singleton says Dev Agents is building a platform they call a next-generation operating system to make AI agents and agentic apps work for everyone, with a specific focus on consumers, since many companies are building agents and agent infrastructure for enterprises. The inspiration, Singleton explains, comes from the early days of mobile, when Singleton began working on smartphones before they were a thing. Singleton is a co-founder alongside two people who came from Android's early product team and from mobile interface design and Chrome. Singleton says the team are enthusiasts for the problem of inventing the right patterns to apply a new technology to people at scale, such as permissions models and application affordances, and, in Singleton's own work, getting the right interface onto a watch.

At Stripe, Singleton says, as models like GPT-4 arrived, Singleton applied them to business problems, building what Singleton calls some of the world's first AI agents, before anyone used the term: an LLM perceiving data, reasoning and taking action. Singleton became obsessed with the idea that this is as significant a breakthrough as early mobile and began tinkering at nights and in the evenings. Many problems to be solved were analogous to the earlier ones. Singleton argues for a place where agents and agentic apps can live, have context on the user and work together, with privacy and security solved in a way that creates real value. It is also a two-sided marketplace like early mobile: developers need access to many people, and people need access to the experiences developers and creators craft.

followups.question: Is the product infrastructure, with a consumer seeing something like an airline agent that a developer built?
answer: Singleton clarifies that Dev Agents is a company name, not a product name. The company is building the platform people will use to find and use agents and agentic apps, and eventually to access experiences others craft. It also has to build the tools and experience for developers and creators to make powerful, valuable agents, and make them accessible to people.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: The AI industry is a war zone. How do you out-compete big names like OpenAI?
answer: Singleton points to early mobile, where many expected Nokia and Sony Ericsson to win on first-mover advantage. They did well early, but mobile needed new paradigms, and the iPhone and Android had to come along. So Singleton does not think the earliest appliers of a technology are the foregone winners. Singleton says Dev Agents takes a very differentiated approach from anything currently in the market but is not ready to share what it is, so that claim is unverified here. Singleton says the team thought less about what other companies are doing and more about what people need, which use cases matter, and how to unlock compounding value when multiple developers' agents can work together for people.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: How different is Singleton's day-to-day now from the first time as a frontline manager?
answer: Quite different, Singleton says, mainly because of the experience and lessons since. Singleton is applying much of what was discussed: stepping onto the balcony periodically to see how everything works, and putting far more energy into preparing for each week and making sure the team knows the most important things to work on. Early in their career it was more a matter of following your nose to the most obvious next thing. Singleton also finds much that is similar, so it feels a little like home and also like a wonderful new challenge. Singleton would not want to work on anything else, believes this is a profound technological leap, and says the work is hard but rewarding, with a lot of type two fun being created now.
blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: Looking back like an incident retrospective, what went well in Singleton's career?
answer: Singleton starts with luck in early choices. Landing at Symbian was formative and, in Singleton's words, fairly random, so Singleton is not sure what others can take from it. The bigger factor, Singleton says, was always making sure they were learning, which explains the long stay at Google and the enjoyable time at Stripe. Singleton also moved teams within companies specifically to learn outside the comfort zone.

As an example, Singleton worked on mobile at Google before Android. There was a weekend, which Singleton remembers clearly, when mobile search queries exceeded desktop queries, a wake-up call for the company. The small side team building mobile things decided to disband and push that work out into the rest of the company. Singleton's default path would have been to join the Android team, which they later did. Instead, Singleton decided the best thing to learn then was ads, because Singleton had no idea how Google made money. Already fairly senior, Singleton joined an organization whose people had mostly grown up in it, and had to learn at a tremendous rate. Singleton now understands the auction systems and the publisher and advertiser business model, and would not without that leap.

followups.question: Is there anything you regret?
answer: Singleton says there are many things they would do differently and has been transparent about some of them, such as being a pretty lousy early manager who focused on making people happy instead of on impact. As an early-career engineer, Singleton often did not speak up in meetings, assuming managers and their managers knew it all and had it sorted. Singleton says the people with the most context are those building at the one-foot level. In many meetings Singleton thought the senior people were wrong but assumed they must know, when Singleton knew because they were doing the work.

Now that Singleton has been the senior person in those rooms, they wish they had built a culture in which people speak up. Singleton's mental model is that everyone is just a human who can only hold so much in their own head, so if you are the expert and really know something, assume they may be wrong and speak up. In every company Singleton worked at, Singleton says, this is rewarded, and Singleton rewards it in the organizations they lead. If you are in an organization that patently does not reward it, Singleton says, perhaps work somewhere else, but most good companies are not like that.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

followups.question: Is one way to tell a company rewards speaking up that titles are less in your face?
answer: Singleton says there is no hard-and-fast rule. When Singleton joined Google in 2005 or 2006, most entry-level hires were given the title member of technical staff, the point being that levels would not be publicly discernible, so people listen to your ideas rather than your title. Singleton thinks that trait is common to organizations that work that way, but it is not the only sign. Another good sign is seeing people speak up, make good points, be listened to, and be encouraged to speak again. On the host's guess that Bell Labs was the source of the title, Singleton agrees it was probably the progenitor, noting the family tree of practices in the industry.
followups.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: Is there a book that really affected your career?
answer: Singleton names High Output Management by Andy Grove, former CEO of Intel. Singleton says that almost every way of working they met at Google and assumed Google had invented turned out to have come from Grove, including OKRs and how to run efficient one-to-ones. It is a short book, which Singleton read on a flight from London to Mountain View, and a bit of a page turner. Singleton accepts that some of it may no longer make sense but says reading it was a pivotal moment in thinking differently about how to run everything at work.
blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: Is there a habit that had a lasting impact across your career?
answer: Singleton describes a planning habit. For a long time Singleton just did whatever arrived: emails, calendar invitations, and one-to-ones already scheduled, so the calendar and inbox ruled them, even when goals existed. Singleton realised that was backwards and began, many years ago during the Google period, to write a to-do list for each week. A week is, in Singleton's experience, the right level of granularity. On Sunday nights Singleton asks what would have to be done for it to have been a great week and writes it down. The document is called the rocket doc, with a rocket emoji as soon as Google Docs supported emojis, to convey the energy wanted. During the week, rather than going to the inbox or calendar, Singleton goes to the rocket doc to decide what to do next.

Later, Singleton shared the document with executive assistants, which Singleton calls a cheat code. The shared goal was for Singleton to spend time on those things, so by mid-day Tuesday an assistant might ask how it was going and chase Singleton to do the intended work, and help shape the calendar around it.

Singleton adds a second habit, exercise. Whenever Singleton found themselves grumpy and unhappy at work, it was often because they had forgotten to exercise. If you are in a funk at work, Singleton suggests making sure you work out a few times a week.
blocks.speaker: David Singleton

blocks.question: What advice would you give your younger self, just graduated and about to enter the industry?
answer: Singleton would repeat the earlier lesson. When you know something and assume it is because you are not the person in charge, speak up. Singleton believes good things happen when you do, and that doing it even more would have produced more good things in the roles Singleton held.
blocks.speaker: David Singleton
